prize_parts.citation: For the development of base editing, the programmable chemical conversion of single DNA bases without double-strand cleavage

statement.case_for: After reading all eight opening ballots I still hold base editing first. It is the one shortlisted candidacy that is a clearly attributable invention with a stated chemical mechanism: a nucleobase deaminase tethered to a Cas9 nickase, with the adenine editor requiring a deaminase evolved to act on DNA, a deaminase that has no natural counterpart. Support is also the broadest on the table, with four top-three placements from members with quite different backgrounds (Aili, Chabes, Linke and myself). It is confirmed by many independent laboratories and has reached first clinical use. The Liu, Komor, Gaudelli trio follows the actual sequence of the work: the concept and cytosine editor, then the adenine editor. That gives a clean three-person configuration without a line-of-work problem.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the increment over the 2020 CRISPR prize. A committee could reasonably see base editing as an engineering extension of an already-recognized platform, and treat the clinical record as too young for a second genome-editing award. There is also an unresolved priority question over Kondo and Nishida's independent cytidine deaminase fusion (Target-AID), which a three-person Liu-led trio would leave out. Somfai ranked this candidacy only eighth, so the case for it is not yet shared by the whole committee.

responses.point: Linke places nanopore sequencing first as a clean physical principle (ionic current blockade) turned into long-read sequencing, and he proposes the single laureate Liu for base editing as third.
responses.response: I agree that nanopore sensing is physically elegant and the field is mature. My difficulty is the one Linke himself names: credit is spread across Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Bayley and Akeson. The decisive ratcheting step is Akeson's, the engineered pore is Bayley's, and the founding idea is Deamer and Branton's. A three-person cut leaves out at least two people whose claims are comparable to those named. Base editing gives us a cleaner attribution. I also disagree with a Liu-only prize. Komor and Gaudelli each made a distinct, experimentally demanding chemical step, and the adenine editor in particular rests on directed evolution that Gaudelli led. I would keep three names unless the committee prefers to narrow the citation.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks phase separation first and calls it a new organizing principle of cell chemistry, with Hyman, Brangwynne and Rosen as the credited core.
responses.response: I take the physical-chemistry argument seriously, and I would support it as an alternative. My reservation is the one Aqvist concedes in his maturity note: whether many in-vivo condensates are truly phase-separated liquids is still debated, and the link to function is uneven. A prize citation would have to state what has been established, and today that statement is weaker than for base editing. The Brangwynne and Hyman 2009 observation is also a founding observation rather than a mechanism, and Rosen's quantitative framework is a different kind of contribution. I would want the expert report to say how far the quantitative physics has actually been tested in cells before I move this above base editing.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalysed C-N coupling first. He sees it as the clearest general method on the list that changed how chemists work, with Buchwald and Hartwig as a clean pair, and ranks base editing only eighth.
responses.response: Buchwald-Hartwig amination is a strong, fully mature candidacy and the two-person attribution is clean. I accept that. I note that the 2010 cross-coupling prize already recognized palladium-catalysed coupling, so the committee would have to judge whether C-N coupling adds enough beyond it, in the same way that I am asked whether base editing adds enough beyond CRISPR. I do not think the two cases are symmetric, though. Base editing introduces a new chemical function, deamination of a base in situ on genomic DNA, whereas C-N coupling extends an established bond-forming strategy. I would be interested in how the expert report weighs this, and I keep it as a serious competitor in a two-part prize.

responses.point: Chabes ranks base editing first on the original chemistry of deaminase fusion and the evolved adenine deaminase. He ranks Solexa sequencing second as overdue transformative chemistry.
responses.response: I agree on the base editing case. On Solexa sequencing, the Balasubramanian and Klenerman pair is clear, but as Chabes notes, Rothberg, Ju and Mayer have legitimate claims to other next-generation sequencing technologies. The committee would need a very carefully bounded citation, and the competing claims are exactly the kind of priority problem I would want resolved before it is a prize configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards base editing as a sufficient increment over the 2020 CRISPR-Cas9 prize.
Whether Kondo and Nishida's independent Target-AID work requires a different configuration, including a fourth or fifth name, and how the three-person limit would apply.
What the expert reports say about clinical maturity of base editing compared with the mature PROTAC and lipid nanoparticle fields.
Whether a two-part prize (for example base editing together with a mature mechanism-based candidacy) would be better than a single achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. I note only that Xiaodong Zou is my Stockholm University colleague, which is not a conflict with any candidate. As Secretary I have a procedural role and no scientific tie to the listed names.
